content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes the use of a knowledge graph to improve the detection of semantic concepts encoded in the network. This is done mainly to improve the interpretation of the model and explanations of its predictions.

Towards this goal the idea of Scoping Core Concepts (SCC) and Indetified Core Concepts (ICC) is put forward.

The proposed method is validated on the ADE20K and Opensurfaces datasets and over several CNN architectures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ Code and data will be released
+ Extracted insights are used to improve performance of the method being explained.

- Presentation is opaque
- Limited to the last convolutional layer of the tested CNN architectures.
- Re-introduced terminology
- Not self-contained
- Limitations are barely discussed.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity
The manuscript has several aspects (ambiguous terminology, similar & unused variables) that hinder clarity.

Quality
There some aspects that affect the perceived quality of the paper:
- Some relevant aspects are delegated to the supplementary material.
- Limitations of the proposed method are lightly addressed

Novelty
While providing some interesting ideas. The manuscript seems to be an extension of CEN (Mu & Andreas, 2020).

Reproducibility
On the one hand, code is released which is positive. On the other hand, description of experimental protocols followed to validate the method is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The manuscript explores the tasks of interpreting the features/information encoded in a model and use these insights to explain the predictions made by the model. In this regard, I find a strength of the manuscript the fact that its explores the interpretation task indicated above which compared to the explanation task is less explored.
In addition a procedure is proposed to exploit the insights obtained by the proposed method to improve the performance of the model being explained/interpreted. I would consider this added value to the paper since it provides actionable ideas on what to do with the insights obtained in the interpretation/explanation task.
Finally, the fact that code is released is a plus for this work since that could contribute to the reproducibility of the reported results and future empirical comparisons. 

My concerns with the paper are the following:

-C1: At some points the terminology is ambiguous. For instance, the term "concept" seem to refer to different things across Sec. 2.2 and 2.3.

-C2: The addressed problem and proposed methods are presented in a very detailed manner. At points the level of detail is too saturating that affects clarity.
For instance, in Sec. 2.3, several components are introduced in some cases using the same variable letters but with different sub/upper indices. Some of these variables are never used beyond their definition. These redundant elements not only take space in the paper but also saturate the reader with content to the point of hindering the understanding of the proposed method.

-C3: At the beginning of Sec, 3.1 it is stated that Eq.1 can estimate general neuron behavior (at the dataset level) which may not be relevant in the prediction made for a given image example. For completeness, it would be good to further elaborate on what are the grounds of this observation.

-C4: Sec. 3.2 introduces Scoping Core Concepts,. From their definition, these SCCs seem to be nothing more that the intersection of the "concepts" (objects) annotated for a given scene class and the KG. To address the generality, and some weaknesses, of SCCs, Identifier Core Concepts (ICCs) are introduced. Unfortunately I find the way they are defined somewhat unclear. Given their apparent importance, I would advice improving the definition of ICCs.

-C5: Sec. 3.3 introduces "With-Prediction Explanations (WPEs)". These WPEs seem to be nothing more than standard "explanations" as usually referred to in the literature.
I would suggest adopting existing terminology instead of introducing new terminology that may lead to confusion.

-C6: In the evaluation of core concepts (SeC. 4.2), it is unclear how the concepts were actually "disabled". Was this done by setting them to zero? or perhaps by a random value? Is there any motivation for following a particular procedure?
Moreover, in the comparison done wrt. ACE the focus is mostly on ICC concepts, which begs the question on why this is the case. For completeness I would suggest also adding to the comparison the results obtained via the proposed SCCs.
In this comparison it is stated that different from ACE which detects independent concepts, the concepts identified by the proposed method are more related with each other. I find this somewhat contradictory to the library example in Figure 6 where the concepts detected by both methods are very similar.

-C7: Comparison with respect to existing methods is limited. There is a qualitaive comparison with the outputs produced by ACE and a qualitative comparison of the effect of different embedding techniques on interpretability (Table 6). While the paper addresses the interpretation of neurons and explanation of model predictions, it is hard to assess how the proposed method is better than existing methods in the literature addressing these problems.

-C8: In Sec. 4.5 (first part), it is stated that results on the OpenSurfaces dataset do not show much improvement, and the this might be due to the fact that that dataset is annotated with fewer concepts (32), which limits the detection ability of neurons. Do this means that for the proposed method to work a dense annotation of concepts is required? is there a way to characterize how many and what types of concepts must be annotated for the proposed to work in an effective manner?

-C9: While the paper presents a significant amount of experiments, the description of the followed experimental protocols is largely delegated to the supplementary material. This is undesirable since it not only hinders an important part of the validation process of the proposed method but also makes the paper not self-contained. In this regard, a better balance must be found between the amount of experiments and their description & discussion.

- C10: The proposed method seems to be limited to the interpretation of the neurons on the last convolutional layer of a given architecture. I would find the potential impact of the proposed method greater if its capabilities would have been assessed on the interpretation of the  complete architecture and not only the last convolutional layer.


MINOR
- In Sec. 2.3, images are referred to by the term x_i in Section 3.1 now the term d is used. 
- Performance metric reported in the tables is not specified

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments. Following your comments, we have carefully revised the paper.
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments.

Comment 1: At some points the terminology is ambiguous. 
Response 1: Thanks for point this out. We optimize the presentation of section 2.2 and 2.3.

Comment 2: The addressed problem and proposed methods are presented in a very detailed manner.
Response 2: Thanks for your comment. As suggested, we revise the section 2.3 and remove some useless variables.

Comment 3: At the beginning of Sec, 3.1 it is stated that Eq.1 can estimate general neuron behavior (at the dataset level) which may not be relevant in the prediction made for a given image example. 
Response 3: Thanks for comment. We add further elaborate on what are the grounds of this observation in section 3.1.

Comment 4: Sec. 3.2 introduces Scoping Core Concepts,. From their definition, these SCCs seem to be nothing more that the intersection of the "concepts" (objects) annotated for a given scene class and the KG. 
Response 4: Thank you for your comment. We will improve the definition of ICCs.

Comment 5: Sec. 3.3 introduces "With-Prediction Explanations (WPEs)". These WPEs seem to be nothing more than standard "explanations" as usually referred to in the literature.
Response 5: Thank you for your comment. As suggested, we will adopt existing terminology for the section "With-Prediction Explanations (WPEs)".

Comment 6: In the evaluation of core concepts (SeC. 4.2), it is unclear how the concepts were actually "disabled".  Moreover, in the comparison done wrt. ACE the focus is mostly on ICC concepts, which begs the question on why this is the case. 
Response 6: Sure, following existing work, we set them to zero to disable concepts. In left of Figure 6, all the concepts in graph are detected by the model and we only display some of them with green box, and all the concepts are easily understandable by human. For the right of the Figure 6, we only display the concepts with top scores, and some of them are detected part of the concepts, such as bookcase and floor.

Comment 7: Comparison with respect to existing methods is limited. There is a qualitaive comparison with the outputs produced by ACE and a qualitative comparison of the effect of different embedding techniques on interpretability (Table 6). While the paper addresses the interpretation of neurons and explanation of model predictions, it is hard to assess how the proposed method is better than existing methods in the literature addressing these problems.
Response 7: Thanks for your comment. The results in Table 6 are quantitative comparison on interpretability which can assess the proposed method is better than existing methods. In Table 6, the gains of different embedding techniques means the improvement compared to the state-of-the-art method. And our TransE-based embedding with 168 clusters achieve the best performance. In addition, would you recommend any method for verifying these problems?

Comment 8: In Sec. 4.5 (first part), it is stated that results on the OpenSurfaces dataset do not show much improvement. Do you means that for the proposed method to work a dense annotation of concepts is required? is there a way to characterize how many and what types of concepts must be annotated for the proposed to work in an effective manner?
Response 8: Thanks for your comment. The reason why the results on Opensurfaces dataset do not show much improvement, and this might be due to the fact that Opensurfaces mainly focuses on annotating the surface property, such as material, which makes the core concept of different scenes with limited differentiation. For example, concepts painted, wood will be core concepts for most scenes, such as living_room, family_room, office and staircase. For the question “how many and what types of concepts must be annotated for the proposed to work?”, from our experiments, we find the core concepts which we proposed not only help to improve the model prediction explanation, but also can effectively change the model performance. So the core concepts need to be annotated for identifying the scenes and will help the model decision process. 

Comment 9: While the paper presents a significant amount of experiments, the description of the followed experimental protocols is largely delegated to the supplementary material. 
Response 9: Thanks for point this out. We will reorganize the experimental structure, and make a balance between the amount of experiments and their description & discussion.

Comment 10: The proposed method seems to be limited to the interpretation of the neurons on the last convolutional layer of a given architecture. 
Response 10: We chose the final layer for explanation mainly for two reasons: (1) following the observations of existing work, when representation in higher layers, the linear/sequential information decreases, while the availability of hierarchical information for model prediction increases; (2) to make a fair comparison with existing work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors proposed to a framework to incorporate concepts from a knowledge graph into explanations for convolutional neural networks. In particular, the authors proposed "core concepts" (scoping core concepts and identifier core concepts), which are concepts associated with a particular class in both the knowledge graph and the images of that class. The authors also proposed consistency/difference/similarity metrics to measure how aligned/different/similar the concepts learned by a neuron (measured by NetDissect or MinMax-NetDissect) are to the core concepts of a class. Finally, the authors conducted a series of experiments to validate their framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Novelty: The idea of integrating concepts from a knowledge graph to explain a neural network is novel. The proposed MinMax-NetDissect, and the metrics for evaluating the consistency/difference/similarity between concepts learned by a neuron and core concepts of a class, are also interesting ideas.

Weaknesses:

- Clarity: This paper is very difficult to read. Several key concepts are not well explained. I had a hard time trying to understand the definition for "identifier core concepts."
- Experiments: It is also not clear to me how the authors evaluated their explanations, due to poor writing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper's clarity and quality is poor. There is some novelty. Since the paper lacks clarity, I cannot judge its reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the strengths and weaknesses of the paper, I do not believe that the paper can be published in its current state.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a knowledge-aware neuron interpretation method to 1) measure the association of concepts with respect to image scenes and 2) analyze solutions for prediction explanation and model manipulation. The proposed method can be used to explain scene classification.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strength**

1 Using a knowledge graph in the explanation is an interesting idea, and the paper shows the usefulness of a knowledge graph, especially in helping the understanding of humans.

2 The proposed explanation could help to correct the original model's error and improve the performance.

**Weaknesses**

1 Fidelity of the explanation. The knowledge graph is treated as a ground truth during the explanation, while the model may not use any object or concept in the ConceptNet. For instance, the scene classification model may use the local color, texture, the whole illumination, or even the background (non-object) as core logic to make the decision. The proposed method could not cover the explanation of these cases.

2 Missing the relationship between objects. A model may not use the existence of objects but their spatial relationship or correlation of them with the background. The proposed method could not be used to explain reasons outside of the predefined knowledge graph.
Please consider comparing your method with "A Peek Into the Reasoning of Neural Networks: Interpreting with Structural Visual Concepts, CVPR 2021" which consider the relationship between objects (concepts) during the explanation.

3 Generalization. The author claim it is a method of image classification (title) while only showing experiments and method of scene classification (a little bit overclaiming). The proposed method needs a predefined knowledge graph, which may be hard to apply to the general image classification task.

4 Time and effort cost. If the user wants to modify one image error, how long will it take? It looks like the method needs a lot of extra training or effort to explain even a single image.
content.summary_of_the_review: The reviewer was curious about the feedback on the previous concerns and questions.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.title: Thank you for your valuable comments. Following your comments, we have carefully revised the paper.
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments.

Comment 1: Fidelity of the explanation. The knowledge graph is treated as a ground truth during the explanation, while the model may not use any object or concept in the ConceptNet. 
Response 1: Thank you for your comments. In our setting, images have pixel-level annotations, and each concept is indexed by the pixels (i, j). So we explain the model predictions by identifying concepts that closely approximate neuron behavior. In fact, we also have the color annotations, but we do not use it for two reasons: (1) color is more general information in image. For instance, there are 11 colors in dataset ADE20K, and each image has an average of 9 colors; (2) the color is not easy to understand by human compared the other concepts, like bed, chair and tree.

Comment 2: Missing the relationship between objects. A model may not use the existence of objects but their spatial relationship or correlation of them with the background. The proposed method could not be used to explain reasons outside of the predefined knowledge graph. 
Response 2: During finding core concepts for scene, we use the concept relationship in ConceptNet to help find the related concepts. Thank you for recommending this related paper (VRX) on interpreting classification NNs. As such, we have introduced this paper in introduction section in revised paper, and we have two observations: (1) this work is based on the work ACE, and we already compare our method to ACE in section 4.2; (2) However, many concepts generated by these methods are still difficult for human to understand.

Comment 3: Generalization.  The proposed method needs a predefined knowledge graph, which may be hard to apply to the general image classification task.
Response 3: Thank you for point this out. Following your suggestion, we change the title to “Explaining  Scene Classification through Knowledge-aware Neuron Interpretation”. Our method dose not need a predefined knowledge graph, and can easily apply to the general image classification task.

Comment 4: Time and effort cost. 
Response 4: For model prediction, our method does not need extra training. For modifying one image error, we propose three strategies: (1) Neuron Identification using CC does not need training phase; (2) Re-training using CC only introduces the CC to objective of the original model which will not introduce more parameters; (3) Re-training using WEP needs to fine-tune on the classical SVM.
